newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD sees better French GDP, EMU targets in reach.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees better French GDP, EMU targets in reach.

text.p: French economic growth should pick up sharply this year and next but the country will need onetime budget measures in 1997 to meet deficit targets for a single European currency, says an OECD report released on Thursday.

The generally upbeat report said recent structural reforms coupled with a big fall in interest rates and a better international economic environment would propel France to growth of 2.5 percent this year, up from 1.3 percent in 1996.

"The sharp easing in monetary conditions and the improvement in the international environment should set the stage for a stronger growth performance in the next two years (1997-98)," the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said.

The report, prepared in December but released on Thursday, predicted a public deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio of 3.2 percent in 1997 but added that the 3.0 percent required under the Maastricht treaty on European monetary union was within reach.
"Even if, as foreseen by the OECD's projection, there is some deficit slippage, there should be room to take the measures needed to bring it back on track," the report said.

France has already resorted to exceptional measures to cut its deficit, transferring 37.5 billion francs from France Telecom to the national accounts in the 1997 budget. In 1996 the government froze spending credits to meet its budgetary targets.

The OECD output forecast is higher than the government's official prediction of 2.3 percent growth this year. Finance Minister Jean Arthuis has said several times recently that prediction should be seen as a floor.

But the report was more sombre on the jobs outlook in France, and said it expects unemployment to remain at 12 percent through 1998 with the bulk of that due to structural rigidities which it advised France to ease.

The OECD's forecasts did not take into account the rise in the dollar of some 10 percent since December which finance ministry officials said could add as much as 0.5 percent to French GDP growth over two years if it were sustained.
Arthuis has expressed satisfaction with the U.S. unit's rise and, while remaining cautious, has called the stronger dollar a positive factor for France.
Finance ministry officials welcomed the OECD report and said they viewed it as an "overall positive assessment of our economic policies".
"We see the report as an invitation to continue on the path of reforms and deficit cutting," said one official.

But the stronger growth will not free France from the grip of its jobs crisis, the OECD said. Unemployment in France currently stands at a record 12.7 percent and remains a major problem for the government.

The report repeated suggestions that France should increase the flexibility of its labour markets to boost employment. It said that because of "substantial structural impediments in the functioning of the labour markets" unemployment would stay high.

"Overall, unemployment should fall over the medium term due to the reduction in cyclical unemployment, while the measures taken in recent years, in particular the reduction in the cost of unskilled labour, should reduce structural unemployment. That said, the structural component is likely to remain sizeable," the report said.
The report put the level of structural unemployment in France at between nine and 10.5 percent.
